children: The S&P 500 enters the shortened Labor Day trading week with an uncomfortable nine-year record.

The index fell on the first trading day after Labor Day every year from 2017 through 2025, according to Bluekurtic Market Insights. Tuesday will test whether Wall Street's seasonal losing streak extends into 2026.
Weakness frequently lasted beyond Tuesday. The S&P 500 finished the entire four-day week higher in only three of those nine years.
In 2024, the index dropped 2.1% on Tuesday before ending the week down 4.2%. In 2020, it opened with a 2.8% decline and finished 2.5% lower.
The pattern is not automatic. The index gained 3.6% during Labor Day week in 2022 after initially slipping 0.4%. It also advanced 1.8% in 2019 despite beginning with a 0.7% loss.
The longer record remains unfavorable. Across Labor Day weeks from 2000 through 2025, the S&P 500 produced an average four-day return of negative 0.4%, while its median return was negative 0.8%.
What the Labor Day Streak Means for Investors

Seasonality can influence trading because vacation-thinned liquidity, portfolio repositioning and September's historically difficult reputation may amplify market moves. However, a calendar pattern does not identify what will drive any specific decline.

The nine-year streak is attention-grabbing but represents a small sample. Investors should therefore treat it as a risk-management signal rather than a reason to automatically sell SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) or Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO).
Traders expecting weakness could watch ProShares Short S&P 500 ETF (SH), which seeks inverse daily exposure, but its daily reset makes longer holding periods more complicated.

This week's direction will ultimately depend on fresh economic data, bond yields and changing interest-rate expectations. If the S&P 500 breaks the streak, it would weaken the seasonal signal. Another Tuesday decline, however, could encourage defensive positioning and reinforce September's reputation as a difficult month for stocks.

title: S&P 500 Investors Brace for Brutal Holiday Pattern
